pedagogy.summary: Hundredths extend the tenfold structure of place value one level deeper: split each tenth into ten equal parts and you get hundredths, so 1/10 ÷ 10 = 1/100 and 100 hundredths make one whole. The pivotal idea is the NESTING — a hundredth is a tenth of a tenth, ten hundredths rebuild one tenth (10/100 = 1/10). Children must hold that a hundredth is SMALLER than a tenth even though 100 is a bigger number than 10; the whole-number bias that 'more parts means bigger' is the central obstacle. Build hundredths by repeated tenfold partitioning on a length or a 10×10 grid, not by cutting a whole into 100 pieces in one go, so the recursive ten-in-one structure is felt.
bestPractices: Derive hundredths by subdividing a tenth, not the whole: take one tenth of a strip and cut it into ten — each piece is a hundredth — so the child sees 1/10 ÷ 10 = 1/100 and that ten hundredths rebuild the tenth.

Use the 10×10 (hundred) grid and a length/number-line model together: the whole grid = 1, one column/row = 1/10, one small square = 1/100; shading shows 100 hundredths in the whole and 10 in each tenth.
Count in hundredths across the tenth boundary aloud — 8, 9, 10, 11, 12 hundredths — and stop to name 10 hundredths as also 1 tenth, so the 10/100 = 1/10 equivalence is explicit.
Confront the whole-number bias directly: put one tenth beside one hundredth and ask which is bigger and why, surfacing the 'but 100 > 10' intuition so it can be overturned.
Anchor to prior tenths work — just as tenths come from dividing by 10, hundredths come from dividing again by 10 — making place value a repeatable action, not a new fact per column.
keyRepresentations: Length / number line from 0 to 1/10 subdivided into 10 hundredths
A tenth-strip physically cut into ten hundredth-pieces (1/10 ÷ 10 = 1/100)
Place-value nesting diagram: whole → tenths → hundredths, each ten-for-one
commonMisconceptions: Whole-number bias on the denominator: believing a hundredth is bigger than a tenth 'because 100 is bigger than 10'.
Not coordinating the nesting — treating 10 hundredths and 1 tenth as different, unrelated amounts.
Believing hundredths can only be made by cutting the whole into 100 at once, not by subdividing tenths (missing the recursive ×10 structure).
Losing count across the tenth boundary (after 9 hundredths, not seeing 10 hundredths = 1 tenth).
Thinking 'hundredths' refers to the large number 100 rather than to tiny parts of a whole.

learn.summary: Build hundredths by subdividing a tenth again by ten, so children feel the recursive tenfold nesting: a hundredth is a tenth of a tenth (1/10 ÷ 10 = 1/100), ten hundredths rebuild one tenth (10/100 = 1/10), and 100 hundredths make one whole. The central obstacle is whole-number bias — believing a hundredth is bigger than a tenth 'because 100 > 10' — so comparing a single tenth against a single hundredth is a strongly recommended way to confront it. Derive hundredths by splitting a tenth, not by cutting the whole into 100 at once.

activities.title: Split a tenth into ten hundredths
feedback: When a child counts past 9 hundredths without naming 10 hundredths as 1 tenth, pause at the boundary and watch the ten small pieces reassemble into exactly one tenth; say '10 hundredths = 1 tenth' together.

If a child says the hundredth is bigger 'because 100 is bigger than 10', place the one hundredth against one tenth so the size difference is plain, and explain that splitting the same whole into more equal parts makes each part smaller.
If a child denies the split pieces are hundredths, show that each of the ten tenths would hold ten such pieces, so 100 of them fill the whole, and name the repeatable 'divide by 10 again' action.
activities.rationale: Deriving hundredths by subdividing a tenth (rather than cutting the whole into 100 in one go) makes the recursive ×10 place-value structure an action the child performs, which the curriculum frames as hundredths arising from dividing tenths by ten. Directly comparing one tenth with one hundredth targets the documented whole-number bias.
sourceClaims: Whole-number bias — drawing false analogies with whole numbers, so that a larger number of digits or a larger denominator is taken to mean a larger quantity — is the central, well-documented obstacle when children extend place value to decimal parts such as hundredths; place-value reasoning (a hundredth is a tenth of a tenth) must be built rather than a rule given.
Pupils should count up and down in hundredths and recognise that hundredths arise when dividing an object by one hundred and dividing tenths by ten (Year 4 statutory content).
learnerActions: Start with a strip that is one whole, already partitioned into ten equal tenths.
Take a single tenth and cut (or subdivide) it into ten equal pieces; name one piece 'a hundredth' and write 1/10 ÷ 10 = 1/100.

Work out how many of these small pieces would fill the whole strip: each of the ten tenths holds ten hundredths, so 10 × 10 = 100. Connect this to 'a hundredth is one of a hundred equal parts of the whole'.
Count aloud in hundredths across the tenth boundary — 8, 9, 10, 11, 12 hundredths — and pause at 10 hundredths to say it is also 1 tenth.
Lay one hundredth directly beside one tenth and describe how much smaller the hundredth is.
activities.intendedInsight: Hundredths come from dividing a tenth again by ten; ten hundredths rebuild one tenth and 100 hundredths make one whole. A hundredth is smaller than a tenth even though 100 is a bigger number than 10, because the same whole is split into more equal parts.

activities.title: Count in hundredths across the tenth boundary and place them on a line
feedback: If a child places 7/100 by guessing, have them first mark the ten equal gaps between 0 and 1/10, then count to the seventh.
If the count continues '10 hundredths, 11 hundredths' without recognising 10 hundredths as 1 tenth, stop at the boundary and name both.
If a child treats 10 hundredths and 1 tenth as unrelated amounts, overlay them on the grid or line so they coincide.
activities.rationale: Counting across the 10/100 = 1/10 boundary and placing hundredths on a 0-to-1/10 line are the curriculum's stated evidence behaviours and surface whether the equivalence is coordinated or merely recited.
sourceClaims: Pupils should count up and down in hundredths and recognise that hundredths arise when dividing an object by one hundred and dividing tenths by ten (Year 4 statutory content).
learnerActions: Count up and down in hundredths from 3/100 to 12/100, saying each amount aloud.
When the count reaches 10 hundredths, name the equivalent in tenths (10 hundredths = 1 tenth), and note that the pattern continues (20 hundredths = 2 tenths).
On a number line running from 0 to 1/10, mark the equal gaps needed to show hundredths and place 7/100 in the correct spot.
Explain how many equal gaps lie between 0 and 1 tenth and why.
activities.intendedInsight: Counting in hundredths and placing them between 0 and a tenth reinforces that each tenth holds exactly ten hundredths, so the count crosses cleanly into tenths.

activities.title: Predict and compare: which is bigger, a tenth or a hundredth?
feedback: A child predicting the hundredth is bigger 'because 100 beats 10' reveals whole-number bias; use the side-by-side comparison to overturn it, then restate the meaning of a tenth and a hundredth as one of ten and one of a hundred equal parts.
If a child cannot say how many hundredths make a whole, count ten hundredths into one tenth and ten tenths into the whole (100).
If a child answers 'a thousandth' for splitting a hundredth, affirm the repeatable divide-by-ten action; if unsure, revisit how each place is a tenth of the one before.
activities.rationale: Stating the reason before comparing makes the bias diagnostic, and the direct size comparison confronts it in the moment, consistent with research naming whole-number bias as the central obstacle that must be built past rather than told.
sourceClaims: Whole-number bias — drawing false analogies with whole numbers, so that a larger number of digits or a larger denominator is taken to mean a larger quantity — is the central, well-documented obstacle when children extend place value to decimal parts such as hundredths; place-value reasoning (a hundredth is a tenth of a tenth) must be built rather than a rule given.
learnerActions: Before any cutting, predict which is bigger — one tenth or one hundredth — and state the reason.
Then split one tenth into ten and lay a single hundredth against a tenth.
Explain whether the result matches the prediction and why a hundredth is smaller despite 100 being larger than 10.
Answer: how many hundredths make one whole, and how do you know?
Consider: if one hundredth were split into ten equal parts again, what would each tiny piece be called?
activities.intendedInsight: A hundredth is smaller than a tenth; the whole-number intuition that '100 > 10 so a hundredth is bigger' is wrong because splitting the same whole into more equal parts makes each part smaller. The ÷10 action repeats to make even smaller places.

constraints: A 10×10 hundred grid and a length/number-line model are complementary and are recommended together (whole grid/strip = 1, one column or row = 1/10, one small square or gap = 1/100); pairing the two models is the original's preferred approach, though a single well-chosen model can also support the learning.
Derive hundredths by subdividing a tenth, not by cutting the whole into 100 pieces in one go, so the recursive ten-in-one structure is felt.

Whole-number bias is the central obstacle and must be addressed, not merely stated; directly comparing exactly one tenth against exactly one hundredth is the strongly recommended means (the original's named approach), though it is one effective technique rather than the only possible one.

Paper or card strips have real thickness and are physical approximations of the ideal flat fractional length; a screen model shows the idealised zero-thickness version. Either can support this learning; neither is required.

Recognition or ordering tasks (e.g. picking which is bigger from options, filling '10 hundredths = __ tenth') check outcomes but do not by themselves build the nesting insight; use them alongside subdivision work, not as a substitute for the child performing the split.

Optional interaction examples that make the mechanism concrete: a live counter that steps in hundredths and snaps to the 1/10 tick with a flipping '10 hundredths = 1 tenth' label; a size-compare mode dropping one hundredth beside one tenth; zooming between 0 and 1/10 to place several hundredths; a tappable column revealing '1 tenth = 10 hundredths'. These are illustrative, not mandatory.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
One source (DfE National Curriculum, Year 4 Fractions) is marked verified:false in the row; treat its curriculum-statement citation accordingly.

The source establishes whole-number bias as the obstacle to overcome but does not mandate one particular comparison technique; the side-by-side tenth-vs-hundredth comparison is the original's recommended means, presented as strongly recommended rather than the sole valid method.
Using both the grid and the length/number-line model together is the original's recommended representation pairing, not an absolute requirement; a single model can also build the nesting insight.

The legacy entries asserted a conversation 'adds nothing over a manipulative' and that 3D 'adds no conceptual gain'. These comparative/necessity claims are not established by the sources; a narrated or spatial presentation can still support learning. Preserved here only as the observation that this planar structure is naturally shown on a grid/length and that the key move is the child performing the subdivision, not as a claim that other media cannot teach it.

Arithmetic/structure audit: 1/10 ÷ 10 = 1/100, 10/100 = 1/10, and 100 hundredths = 1 whole are all consistent; the evidence range 3/100 to 12/100 correctly crosses the 10/100 boundary. No errors found.

assess.poeTask: Before any cutting, ask the child to PREDICT which is bigger, one tenth or one hundredth, and to say WHY. The stated reason is the diagnostic part — a child predicting the hundredth is bigger 'because 100 beats 10' reveals the whole-number bias. Then split one tenth-strip into ten and lay a single hundredth against a tenth: the hundredth is plainly tiny. Have the child explain the mismatch with their prediction.
probeDeeper: You said 10 hundredths is the same as 1 tenth. How many hundredths make one whole, and how do you know?
Which is bigger, 1 tenth or 1 hundredth — and why, when 100 is bigger than 10?
If I split one hundredth into ten equal parts again, what would each tiny piece be called?
Show me 7 hundredths on a line that runs from 0 to 1 tenth — how many equal gaps do you need, and where does 7 hundredths sit?
assess.correctAnswer: After 9 hundredths comes 10 hundredths, which is the same as 1 tenth; then 11, 12 hundredths. Splitting one tenth into ten gives hundredths (1/10 ÷ 10 = 1/100), because each place is a tenth of the one before; 100 hundredths make one whole.

errorPatterns.pattern: Whole-number bias on the denominator: 'a hundredth is bigger than a tenth because 100 is bigger than 10'.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Overlay one hundredth on one tenth so the hundredth is visibly tiny; re-establish that more, smaller parts means each is smaller. Reteach that a tenth is one of ten equal parts of the whole and a hundredth is one of a hundred.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: When asked which is bigger (tier-2 or probe), picks the hundredth; treats a larger denominator as a larger part.

errorPatterns.pattern: Does not coordinate the nesting — counts to 10 hundredths but treats it as unrelated to 1 tenth ('10 hundredths and 1 tenth are different amounts').
errorPatterns.nextMove: On the grid, watch ten hundredths rebuild exactly one tenth; count across the boundary naming 10/100 = 1/10 each time. Reteach the ten-for-one structure from tenths.
errorPatterns.distractor: 10 hundredths is not the same as 1 tenth.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Cannot give '1 tenth' as another name for 10 hundredths; counts past the boundary without recognising the equivalence.

errorPatterns.pattern: Believes hundredths can only be made by cutting the whole into 100 directly — 'you can't get hundredths by splitting a tenth' — missing the recursive ×10 structure.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Split a tenth into ten and count how many such pieces fill the whole (100); make the repeatable 'divide by 10 again' action explicit. Reteach the tenfold partition from tenths.
errorPatterns.distractor: You can't make hundredths by splitting a tenth — hundredths only come from cutting the whole into 100 pieces.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On the split-a-tenth task, denies the pieces are hundredths or cannot say what they are; sees no link between dividing a tenth and hundredths.

responseLevels.gap: Counts hundredths as a rote sequence but sees no link to tenths, or believes a hundredth is bigger than a tenth. Cannot explain where hundredths come from.
responseLevels.full: Counts across the 10/100 = 1/10 boundary, explains a hundredth as a tenth of a tenth (1/10 ÷ 10 = 1/100) with 100 hundredths in the whole, holds that a hundredth is smaller than a tenth despite 100 > 10, and transfers the ÷10 action to predict thousandths.
responseLevels.partial: Knows 100 hundredths make a whole and can count in hundredths, but cannot explain the tenfold nesting — lists the parts without relating them (does not connect 10 hundredths = 1 tenth or 1/10 ÷ 10 = 1/100).

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Start at 8 hundredths and count up in hundredths past ten: what comes after 9 hundredths, and what is another name for it? Then, if I take one tenth and split it into ten equal parts, what is each part called — and why?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who understands the tenfold nesting counts smoothly across 10/100 and names it as 1 tenth, and explains a hundredth as a tenth of a tenth. A child with whole-number thinking counts '10 hundredths, 11 hundredths' but does not see it equals a tenth, or believes a hundredth is bigger than a tenth because 100 > 10, or insists hundredths can only come from cutting the whole into 100. The second tier ('why') separates a memorised count from grasp of the recursive structure.
